transcript.text: Natural Monopoly & Regulation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-41
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Natural Monopoly & Regulation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A natural monopoly has declining average cost across the relevant market range, making one large producer less costly than several small firms. The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC. Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for average cost that continues falling across the relevant range of market demand.
Marginal-cost pricing expands output toward efficiency but may leave the firm unable to cover average cost.
Average-cost pricing can preserve financial viability but produces less than the efficient quantity.
Evaluate regulation by comparing price, output, efficiency, and the need for subsidy or allowed profit.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse allocative efficiency with break even. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC. Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.
WORKED EXAMPLE: REGULATING A NATURAL MONOPOLY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down and MR slopes down more steeply. MC is horizontal at 10; ATC declines. Guides show MR meeting MC near quantity 70, where demand is near 27. Demand meets ATC near quantity 115 and price 16. Demand meets MC at quantity 140 and price 10, while ATC at 140 is about 15. The values near 70, 115, 27, 16 and 15 are approximate readings from the marked guides.

Marginal-cost pricing sets demand equal to MC, which the graph shows at 140 units and $10. ATC there is about $15, so the regulated firm would lose about ($15 - $10) x 140 = $700. Average-cost pricing near 115 units and $16 avoids that loss but leaves price above marginal cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
What is the main compromise under average-cost pricing?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Price Discrimination
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-42
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Price Discrimination.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same product when resale can be prevented. Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist. Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable. Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.
The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.
Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to disconnect wtp from first degree efficiency. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING PRICE DISCRIMINATION

A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.
CHECK YOURSELF
Can ordinary group price discrimination increase total welfare?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Market Structure & Product Differentiation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-43
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify Market Structure & Product Differentiation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Monopolistic competition combines many firms and relatively easy entry with differentiated products and limited price-setting power. Entry and exit operate in both models. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry. The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product. Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A market has many sellers and easy entry.
A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments.
A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away.
A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product.
A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION

A city has many coffee shops, entry is relatively easy, and each shop offers a distinct menu and atmosphere. Because customers view the shops as close but imperfect substitutes, each shop faces downward-sloping demand and has limited price-setting power. Those facts identify monopolistic competition.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-44
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN FIRM DECISION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The firm chooses 36 units where MR = MC at $15, then charges $27 on its demand curve. ATC is also $27, so total revenue and total cost are both $27 x 36 = $972. Economic profit is zero, but P > MC shows the outcome is not allocatively efficient.
CHECK YOURSELF
A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-45
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

At 36 units, the firm charges $27 and has ATC of $27. Total revenue is $27 x 36 = $972, and total cost is also $972, so economic profit is zero. With no profit attracting entry and no loss causing exit, the industry is in long-run equilibrium.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does excess capacity measure?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-46
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Advertising can provide information, persuade buyers, build a brand, and change the elasticity or position of a firm's demand curve. The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price. In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales. A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC. The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged.
Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase.
A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand.
A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information.
A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price. In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INFORMATIVE OR PERSUASIVE ADVERTISING?

A pharmacy advertises that a prescription costs $8 and that it stays open until 10 p.m. Buyers can compare stores more easily, so search costs fall; this is informational advertising. A separate campaign associates the brand with status without adding product facts; that campaign is persuasive advertising. Both compete without directly cutting price.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does nonprice competition mean?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Product Variety, Efficiency & Model Limits
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-47
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate Product Variety, Efficiency & Model Limits.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Monopolistic competition trades some cost and allocative efficiency for product variety and differentiated consumer choices. Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain. Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain.
Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs.
Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
Two markets have the same total production cost.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: VARIETY VERSUS EFFICIENCY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The long-run firm produces 36 units at a price and ATC of $27, so economic profit is zero. Marginal cost is only $15, meaning price exceeds MC, and output lies left of minimum ATC. Product variety may benefit consumers, but the model also predicts markup and excess capacity.

Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
WATCH OUT
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MARKET CONCENTRATION

Horizontal axis: Firm or fringe, with categories A, B, C, D and Other; vertical axis: Market share in percent. The five bars have printed values A 38 percent, B 32 percent, C 12 percent, D 9 percent, and Other 9 percent. Other is a separate aggregate category, not labeled as a single firm.

The graph shows market shares of 38%, 32%, 12%, 9%, and 9%. HHI equals the sum of squared shares: 38^2 + 32^2 + 12^2 + 9^2 + 9^2 = 1,444 + 1,024 + 144 + 81 + 81 = 2,774. That value indicates substantial concentration.

Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-49
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume equilibrium is efficient. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NASH EQUILIBRIUM

For each strategy of the other player, mark the action that gives a player the larger payoff. In the displayed matrix, row A against column X gives (9, 9), while switching unilaterally to row B would lower the row player's payoff from 9 to 3. The column player also prefers X to Y when row A is chosen, so (A, X) is a cell of mutual best responses and is a Nash equilibrium.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why must payoff order be stated?

Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-50
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.
The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.
A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
Three firms agree to keep prices high.
WATCH OUT
Do not miss individual incentive to defect. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY CARTELS BREAK DOWN

Horizontal axis: market quantity; vertical axis: price and cost. Demand D slopes down from price 100 at quantity 0 and crosses horizontal MC at price 20 and quantity 40. MR slopes down more steeply from 100 to zero near quantity 25, crossing MC at quantity 20. At quantity 20, demand is near price 60. Values without point guides are approximate readings from the scale.

A cartel acts like one monopolist and selects industry output where industry MR equals MC. On the graph, the downward-sloping MR curve meets the $20 MC line at 20 units. The cartel then uses demand to set price. Each member has an incentive to sell extra units, which makes the agreement unstable.

Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-51
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence examines repeated interaction, credibility, commitments, limit pricing, entry deterrence, continuation incentives, and sequential strategic reasoning. A higher continuation factor increases the weight on future consequences. Cooperation PV is 12.50; cheating path PV is 16.25. Net gain = 25 − 8 − 14 = 3 million. Aggressive competition and predation must be distinguished with evidence.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume every low price is predatory. Net gain = 25 − 8 − 14 = 3 million. Aggressive competition and predation must be distinguished with evidence.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A CREDIBLE THREAT

Sequential game tree; payoffs are ordered Entrant, Incumbent. The Entrant moves first. Stay out ends with payoffs (0, 12). Enter leads to the Incumbent decision node. From that node, Accommodate ends with (6, 7), and Fight ends with (negative 3, 3). Branch labels identify the actions; each payoff belongs to its branch endpoint.

The game tree is solved backward. If entry occurs, the incumbent receives 7 by accommodating and 3 by fighting, so accommodation is the credible response on that branch. Anticipating it, the entrant compares 6 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The subgame-perfect outcome is Enter, then Accommodate.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does low pricing prove predation?

Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-52
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Tacit coordination occurs when firms align behavior without an explicit agreement, while nonprice competition uses quality, service, or advertising rather than price cuts. Advertising can shape demand in both markets. Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price. Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes.
A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical.
Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.
A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume price is irrelevant. Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions. A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RECOGNIZING NONPRICE COMPETITION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price and cost. Demand D has a kink at approximately quantity 20 and price 50: it is steeper to the left and flatter to the right. MR has two downward-sloping segments separated by a gap at quantity 20, from approximately 10 to 32. Horizontal MC is around 37. These are approximate readings, and the MC line is visibly above the top of the MR gap.

The kink in demand occurs near 20 units and a price of $50. Because the marginal-revenue curve has a gap at that output, modest changes in MC around $36 need not change the chosen price or quantity. The model explains price rigidity while reminding us that oligopolists can still compete through quality, service, and advertising.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does parallel pricing prove collusion?

Oligopoly and merger policy weighs the risk of reduced rivalry against verifiable efficiencies, innovation, entry, and consumer effects. Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits. A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses. The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss. Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.
The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.
A concentrated industry has high prices, strong product innovation, and frequent entry by niche rivals.
A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion.
A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate cartel profit with dwl. DWL is the triangle between demand and MC over the lost output. Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING MERGER EFFECTS

A merger raises the HHI and may increase market power, but the statistic alone is not the verdict. Suppose the merged firm can cut marginal cost by $4 per unit and entry remains easy. An antitrust evaluation compares the likely price and output effects of reduced rivalry with the verifiable efficiency and entry evidence before reaching a conclusion.

Does a higher post-merger HHI settle the welfare question?
